reviewNotes: No person has reviewed this file.

What was adapted: Lesson 17 is IM’s Let’s Put it to Work project, with no cool-down, no lesson synthesis and no student summary. IM says it may take more than one class. The plan keeps the usual shape: crux 17.2, with Three Reads, a release frame, and Collect and Display. Where IM has nothing, Premo wrote it: the look-for checks the crux’s closing question instead of a cool-down, and the lesson synthesis is Premo’s. The planning view’s “Do the cool-down” step has nothing of IM’s to show for this lesson.

Story and previous: from IM’s lesson narrative (“applying and integrating many concepts and skills from the past three units”), Lesson 16’s goal (what percentage C is of B), and unit.json’s sections (Let’s Put it to Work is Lesson 17 alone).
Crux is 17.2, as in Premo’s layer. 17.3 (painting time, percentages) carries the other half of goal 1 and is a fair alternative, but it has no IM routine or support.

CLO: imGoal is IM goal 1, verbatim. Function is “explain,” from the goal. unit.json’s language progression lists “interpret” (situations involving measurement, rates, and cost) and “justify” (reasoning about costs and time) for Lesson 17, so there is a progressionNote. Goal 2 (simplifying assumptions) is in the synthesis’s “Can all of these values be correct?” but not in the objective.

Form: how a strong student explains a cost: the paint from the area and the rate, then the containers and the total. It names no task item. Precise terms: “square feet,” “per” and “total cost.” The exemplar and the release frames use IM’s own answer path: 600 ÷ 87.5 ≈ 6.86, so 7 quarts; 1 gallon and 3 quarts cost $67.60; with IM’s $20 kit, $87.60.
Posted sentence uses new numbers: 400 ÷ 90 ≈ 4.4, so 5 quarts; 5 × $8 = $40; with $15 of supplies, $55.
Look-for: there is no cool-down, so it checks the answer to IM’s “Can all of these values be correct?” A reviewer should decide whether 17.3’s first question (24%) is the better check.

Per D1: Three Reads is IM’s own 17.2 support, so the launch card follows IM’s three reads, including adding quantities to the floor plan. MLR 8 frames come at release, which here is after the class agrees on 300 square feet, before paint and cost: the CLO is about the cost. MLR 2 Collect and Display in the synthesis builds in IM’s own moves (D1 option 3): explain the paint first, poll cost ranges, ask “Can all of these values be correct?”, record and display.

Minutes inside 17.2 are estimates on IM’s printed 35 minutes, which IM’s own launch (15 minutes of quiet think time for the area alone, then a debrief) makes tight. IM’s narrative says the times are “intentionally left blank.” The 17.2 cut says how to split it over two days.

17.2 momentIds: m3, m5, m7, within the cap of three. m2 (Three Reads slipping) is not a card; its line is in the launch card’s notes. m4 (yards times feet) is a back-pocket question. m8’s share order is in the synthesis steps. m6 (running Three Reads) is the launch card’s job.
17.2 depends on 17.1 for IM’s $20 painting kit, which the cost answers include. If 17.1 is skipped, the teacher gives the price.
Math checked: see Premo’s notes (300 square feet; 7 quarts; $89.80, $96.30, $87.60; $81.04, $81.06; 24%, 304, 154). The lesson synthesis check: 250 ÷ 100 = 2.5, so 3 cans; 3 × $12 = $36.

NEW (Premo-written, unreviewed): every student’s words and work on the cards, every ifNot, the goingOn lines, the frames by level and their nonverbal ways in, the Sounds like lines, and the whole lesson synthesis.
Non-crux activities carry no language supports (D7).
story: Lesson 17 puts the unit to work. Students plan a painting job: wall area, paint from a rate, cost with a coupon, and time with percentages.
previous: In Lesson 16 students found what percentage one number is of another; today they use that, and unit rates, in one project.

clo.imGoal: Apply rates and percentages to calculate how long it will take and how much it will cost to complete a painting project, and explain (orally) the reasoning.
clo.form: I need ___ quarts, because ___ square feet ÷ ___ square feet per quart is about ___. Buying ___ costs $___, so the total cost is $___.

board.content: We will use rates and percentages to find what a painting project costs.
board.language: We will explain, out loud, how we found the cost, using “square feet,” “per” and “total cost.”

clo.exemplar: I need 7 quarts, because 600 square feet ÷ 87.5 square feet per quart is about 6.9. Buying 1 gallon and 3 quarts costs $67.60, so the total cost is $87.60 with the $20 kit.
clo.lookFor: No cool-down in this lesson. At “Can all of these values be correct?”, a student explains a total cost: the paint from the rate (2 quarts per 175 square feet), the containers, and a matching total, such as $87.60.

posted.sentence: I need 5 quarts, because 400 square feet ÷ 90 square feet per quart is about 4.4. Buying 5 quarts at $8 costs $40, so the total cost is $55 with $15 of supplies.

clo.progressionNote: IM’s unit overview lists “interpret” and “justify” for this lesson. The objective follows the lesson’s own goal: “explain.”

strategies: IM’s list: paint, paint brushes, paint rollers, drop cloths, painter’s tape, mixing sticks, ladder, paint can opener.
Some groups add a cost for each item. IM: hardware stores sell painting kits (brushes, rollers, a tray, a drop sheet) for around $20.
barriers: Some students have never painted a room or seen one painted.
Tool names (roller, drop cloth, painter’s tape) may be new words.
misconceptions: Listing only paint, because the job is unfamiliar.
Adding a price for the paint now; IM leaves that until the amount is known.
backPocket: What might this cost at a hardware store?
activities.grouping: Small groups, each with at least one student who has painted, if possible. IM: poll the class first.
activities.monitor: Listen for tools beyond paint. Record the class list, with costs where you can, and keep it up all lesson.

strategies: Area, wall by wall: east 72, south 65 (80 minus the 15 square foot window), west 51 (72 minus the 21 square foot door), north 76, small wall 36. Total 300 square feet.
Paint: 2 quarts per 175 square feet is 87.5 square feet per quart. Two coats is 600 square feet, so about 6.86 quarts: buy 7.
Containers: 7 quarts ($76.30), 2 gallons ($69.80), or 1 gallon and 3 quarts ($67.60). With IM’s $20 kit: $96.30, $89.80 or $87.60.
Coupon, 20% off quarts only: 7 quarts gives $81.04; 1 gallon and 3 quarts gives $81.06; 2 gallons stays $89.80.
barriers: Floor plans may be new: which lines are walls, the door, the window, the closet.
Mixed units: yards for two walls, feet for the rest; quarts and gallons for paint.
Words such as “coats,” “mirrored closet doors” and “floor-to-ceiling.”
misconceptions: Leaving out a surface: the small wall, the 3 square feet above the door, or the wall above and below the window.
Multiplying yards by feet: 3 × 8 for the east wall.
Planning paint for one coat only, from 300 square feet.
Language: “Ours is right, theirs is wrong,” with no reason for either total.
backPocket: Walk me around the room. Which surfaces get paint?
How many coats? How much wall does that make?
Can both be right? What did each one buy?
activities.grouping: Pairs: quiet think time alone on the area, then partners compare. Class agrees on the area, then each student finishes alone.
activities.monitor: IM: notice who organizes their work methodically and who needs help. Track each pair’s area, then each student’s containers and total.

dependsOn.note: IM’s cost answers include the $20 painting kit from 17.1’s closing. If you skip 17.1, give students that price before question 3.

strategies: Divide, then multiply by 100: \(\frac{72}{300} \boldcdot 100\) is 24%, so the friend is not quite right.
1% first: 3 square feet is 1%, so 72 square feet is 24%.
Time: 96 minutes for 24% is 4 minutes per 1%. The other 76% takes 304 minutes alone, so the friend saved 304 − 150, or 154 minutes.
barriers: 17.3 needs 17.2’s 300 square feet and the east wall’s 72.
“25% finished” is about the painting, not the time.
misconceptions: Counting drying time between coats; the problem counts painting time only.
Saying 25% because the east wall is one of four walls.
Subtracting 150 from 96, or from 400, instead of from the time alone for the rest.
backPocket: Are all four walls the same size?
How many minutes is 1% of the painting?
Which time does the problem count?
activities.grouping: Alone, then pairs: quiet think time, then partners check each other’s work. Each student gets ready to explain their partner’s way.
activities.monitor: Check the first answer before partners move on; IM says the second needs it. Note who finds 1% first and who divides 72 by 300.

release.successCriteria: Name the paint you need with the rate (square feet per quart), the containers you buy, and the total cost.
release.say: Say how much paint, using the rate. Then say how you got your total cost.
talkMoments: Before the coupon question, partners take turns explaining their total cost with Today’s frame.
In the closing discussion, students who chose different containers each explain their total.

developing.frame: I need ___ quarts, because ___ square feet at ___ square feet per quart is about ___. Buying ___ costs $___, so the total cost is $___.
developing.stretch: They say why a different total can also be right.

expanding.frame: I need ___ quarts, because ___ square feet ÷ ___ square feet per quart is about ___. Buying ___ costs $___, so the total cost is $___.
expanding.stretch: They explain how the coupon changes which containers to buy.
expanding.nonverbal: Write the chain area, paint, cost, with a unit on each step, before they speak.

steps: Ask 1–2 students how much paint they needed. Scribe their words as said, such as “two coats.” Write “square feet per quart” beside them.
Poll cost ranges, as IM suggests ($85–$89.99, $90–$94.99, $95–$99.99). Then ask, “Can all of these values be correct?”
After quiet think time, call 2–3 students with different containers. Scribe each total as said, with the containers beside it.
Write “total cost” beside their words. Ask how the coupon changes the best buy; students decide, and you scribe.
Leave the board up for 17.3 and the close of the lesson.
synthesis.prompt: Can all of these values be correct? How?
synthesis.sounds: Yes. Both buy 7 quarts of paint for 600 square feet. 7 quarts cost $76.30, but 1 gallon and 3 quarts cost $67.60, so the total cost differs.

rehearsal.name: Do the painting task yourself
rehearsal.where: Before class. Solve the task: wall area, paint for two coats, and the cost.
show: The east wall is 3 yards long.
The south wall is 10 feet long but has a window, 5 feet by 3 feet, that does not need to be painted.
The west wall is 3 yards long but has a door, 7 feet tall and 3 feet wide, that does not need to be painted.

The north wall includes a closet, 6.5 feet wide, with floor-to-ceiling mirrored doors that do not need to be painted. There is, however, a smaller wall between the west wall and the closet that does need to be painted on all sides. The wall is 0.5 feet wide and extends 2 feet into the room.
The ceiling in this room is 8 feet high.
An advertisement about the paint that you want to use reads: “Just 2 quarts covers 175 square feet!” If you need to apply two coats of paint on all the walls, how much paint do you need to buy?

beforeClass: Work 17.2 yourself: the area, the paint for two coats, and two ways to buy it, with and without the coupon.
Find a floor plan of your classroom to display, and a short video of someone painting, in case few students have painted.
For Three Reads in 17.2: display the bedroom plan and its list, with the four questions covered until the third read. Have a marker to add quantities to the plan.
For Collect and Display (MLR 2): clear board space and IM’s cost ranges ready to poll ($85–$89.99, $90–$94.99, $95–$99.99).

cuts.note: Keep it short: one class list, and IM’s $20 painting kit for supplies.
If short of time, do the first question only: is the friend right about 25%? Lost: the time saved, which uses 24% again.
IM says this lesson can take more than one class. If you split it, stop once the class agrees on 300 square feet. Never cut the closing discussion.

ideas: A real project takes steps: the area first, then the paint, then the cost.
A rate links them: 2 quarts per 175 square feet tells how much paint 600 square feet needs.
A percentage compares a part with the whole: the east wall’s 72 of 300 square feet is 24% of the job.
lessonSynthesis.pointTo: Point to the 17.2 board: the different totals and students’ words for how each was found. If you taught 17.3, point to the 24%.

check.question: A fence needs 250 square feet of stain. One can covers 100 square feet and costs $12. What does the stain cost, and why?
